name: Lysosome
short_description: The recycling plant: a membrane bubble full of digestive enzymes that only work in its acidic interior. It breaks down engulfed particles and the cell's own worn-out parts into building blocks the cell reuses.

textbook.1: pass (gemini-2.5-flash-image, accepted on the first attempt; a clean cutaway of a single round lysosome bounded by exactly ONE thin, unbroken steel-blue limiting membrane - no second concentric line anywhere. The lumen is a warm amber-tan wash, visibly heterogeneous and granular: dusty-rose acid-hydrolase granules and irregular grey-brown partly-digested chunks are scattered through it, never a smooth empty bubble. A fine pale-gold fuzzy glycocalyx lining sits just inside the membrane, and small teal-green stalked V-ATPase knobs stud the membrane from the inside. Beside it, its membrane visibly merging into the lysosome's own boundary at one shared seam, a separate pale sky-blue phagosome holds one simple olive rod-shaped bacterium, with rose-red granules starting to spill across the fusing neck. Muted educational palette, thin clean outlines, dark charcoal ground, edge-to-edge fill, no text, no border, no double membrane, no cristae, no ribosome studs, no stacked cisternae, enzymes drawn as granules not tools)

Exactly one smooth steel-blue limiting membrane (never doubled), a densely granular heterogeneous amber lumen packed with rose hydrolase granules and grey-brown partly-digested chunks, a fuzzy pale-gold glycocalyx lining and small teal V-ATPase knobs studding the inner membrane face. The lysosome's fractured membrane visibly merges with a separate pale sky-blue phagosome holding one olive rod-shaped bacterium, with hydrolase granules spilling across the fusing seam. Cool studio microscopy lighting, false-colour palette, edge-to-edge, no text, no border, no double membrane, no cristae)

watercolor.1: pass (gemini-2.5-flash-image, accepted on the first attempt; warm aged paper fills the entire frame edge-to-edge and corner-to-corner with a soft darker wash halo painted directly on the paper behind the subject - no mat, no border, no frame, no sheet-on-a-surface. Fine ink outlines trace exactly ONE limiting membrane washed steel-blue around the lysosome, never a second concentric line. The lumen is washed warm amber-tan and pink, textured with visible rose-red dabs (hydrolase granules) and irregular grey-brown blotches (partly digested content) so it reads as heterogeneous and granular. A fine fuzzy pale-gold line (glycocalyx) runs along the inside of the membrane with small stalked teal-green V-ATPase knobs pointing inward. The lysosome's outline visibly merges with a second, separate, pale sky-blue washed phagosome at one shared painted seam; inside it sits one simple olive rod-shaped engulfed bacterium, with rose dabs and a teal knob crossing into the newly joined space. Fine ink linework over translucent washes, single lysosome and single phagosome, no text, no arrows, no scale bar, no double membrane, no cristae)

reference: pass, with an honest caveat (Wikimedia Commons "Macrophage in the alveolus Lung - TEM.jpg", Public domain, Louisa Howard, Rippel Electron Microscope Facility, Dartmouth College, JEOL 100CX TEM, thin section of mammalian lung tissue - the same public-domain series already used for the nucleus and mitochondrion in this atlas. Viewed directly: a macrophage's lobulated, densely-chromatinized nucleus fills the centre-right, and the surrounding cytoplasm holds several round, moderately-to-highly electron-dense, homogeneously granular bodies without visible cristae - morphologically consistent with lysosomes/dense cytoplasmic granules, exactly what a professional phagocyte like a macrophage is packed with. Caveat stated plainly: the file's own caption does NOT explicitly name any structure as a lysosome (it only mentions the nucleus and 'cytoplasmic organelles, such as golgi and mitochondria'), so this identification rests on general TEM morphology rather than an explicit label, and no engulfed bacterium is visible in this particular frame - it documents a lysosome-rich macrophage, not a phagolysosome caught mid-fusion. Presented as the best available real-world anchor for lysosome ultrastructure, not as photographic proof of the illustrated phagosome-fusion scene. Cleaned with NO image-editing model: a deterministic local crop removed the plain white caption/scale-bar footer bar confined to the bottom ~25px of the 640x480 original, then a centred square crop (455x455) and a Lanczos resize to 1080x1080 (a 2.37x upscale, recorded explicitly in the sidecar) produced the final text-free reference. Nothing was invented, re-illustrated or reframed)
